goal: `mc` left open at a terminal keeps telling the truth. Every 30 seconds the rows that changed are rewritten where they stand, and nothing else on the screen moves — not the scrollback above, not the prompt below, not the cursor in whatever the person was half-way through typing.
contract: **The surface updates; the page is not reprinted.** Martin, 2026-09-02: *"inte laddar om utan själva ytan uppdateras"*. Clearing and redrawing is what `--watch` did on 2026-08-29, and it was removed the same day — *"a page redrawn on a timer is not a live page; the real one comes later"* (`docs/technical/mc-ui.md`). This is that later.

**No alternate screen buffer.** `mc` prints into the terminal's own scrollback and what is above it belongs to the person. A full-screen mode would take the terminal over and give the scrollback back changed.
**A pipe still prints once and exits 0.** Without a TTY nothing loops, nothing moves a cursor, and no escape sequence is written — the rule the page already keeps (`colourFor`, `parsePageArgs`).
**The menu keeps working while the page moves.** A person who has typed `1` and not yet pressed return must not lose it, and must not have it redrawn somewhere else.
**Reads only.** A refresh is `collectPage`, which touches no state but its own two read-through caches. Nothing about being live may make the page start, stop, merge or write anything.
Nothing merges to main without Martin.
out_of_scope: **Making `collectPage` faster.** It is measured below and it is a problem, but it is a different one — and a refresh that cannot keep up is handled here by not blocking on it, not by making it quick.
A live `mc status <name>`. One surface at a time.
Pushing anything from the runner or a session into the terminal. The page reads files; it is not told.
Any interval but 30 s, and any way of configuring it. One number, chosen, until there is a reason for another.

success_criteria.criterion: A row that changes is rewritten in place, and no other row on the screen is written to at all.
success_criteria.check: A unit test over the frame differ: two `renderPageLines` results differing in one row produce a byte sequence that positions the cursor once, writes that row, and returns — asserted on the bytes, with no terminal involved.

success_criteria.criterion: The scrollback above the page is untouched after ten refreshes.
success_criteria.check: In a real terminal: print a marker line, run `mc`, let it refresh ten times, quit, and scroll up. The marker is where it was, once.
In a real terminal: type `1` without pressing return, wait through a refresh, and see the `1` still at the prompt and the cursor after it. Then press return and get that project's workarea.

success_criteria.criterion: A pipe is exactly what it is today.
success_criteria.check: `mc | cat` and `mc --json | cat` print once, exit 0, and their output contains no ESC byte — asserted in `tests/mc/front-door.test.js`.

success_criteria.criterion: A refresh that takes longer than the interval delays the next frame rather than overlapping it.
success_criteria.check: A unit test with a collect that resolves after 45 s of fake time: frames are 45 s apart, never two in flight, and no frame is skipped silently without the page saying so.

documents.label: The page, its sections, and why `--watch` was removed

steps.title: The difference between two frames
steps.done_when: A pure function turns a previous and a next array of lines into the writes that make the terminal show the second, and a test asserts the bytes for an unchanged frame, a one-row change, a shorter frame and a longer one.
instruction: A new module beside `page-render.js` — it knows about terminals, and `page-render.js` deliberately does not. Input: the previous lines, the next lines, and where the page starts relative to the cursor. Output: a string of writes, empty when nothing changed.

The cases that decide the shape. **Unchanged:** no bytes at all, not a redraw of identical text — a terminal that receives nothing is the only way to be sure nothing flickered. **One row changed:** move to that row, clear it to the end of the line, write it. **Fewer rows than before:** the surplus rows are cleared, not left holding an older page. **More rows:** the page has grown past where it started, and the terminal will scroll; this is the case that must be got right or the scrollback is damaged, so decide it deliberately and write down what was decided.

Use `CSI` cursor-position-relative sequences (`\x1b[<n>A`, `\x1b[<n>B`, `\x1b[2K`) rather than absolute positioning: absolute row numbers are wrong the moment anything else writes to the terminal, and the page has no claim on the screen.
Test it as bytes. This is the one part of a live surface that can be tested without a terminal, so it is the part that carries the assertions.
comments: **The renderer already hands back the thing a differ needs**

**The renderer already hands back the thing a differ needs.** `renderPageLines` returns an array of lines and says why in its own header — *"Lines rather than one string, so a test can look at a row without splitting a page apart again"* (`src/mc/page-render.js`). So the frame difference is an array comparison, not a text diff, and it can be a pure function tested with no terminal at all.

The lines carry escape sequences when colour is on, and `paint` already guarantees a coloured row is exactly as wide as its plain twin. Comparing the strings as written is therefore the right comparison: two rows that differ only in colour *are* different rows, and both are one write.
**The page is not 0.1 s any more, and a live one has to survive that**

**The page is not 0.1 s any more, and a live one has to survive that.** `docs/technical/mc-ui.md` records 0.09–0.11 s with both caches hit. Measured 2026-09-02 on a machine with the runner and several sessions on it: `mc --json` took **2.4 s, 2.7 s, 4.8 s** in three consecutive runs, and 3.9–6.6 s in a second set. The plans cache is keyed by the `origin/main` sha, and on a machine where the runner is landing pull requests that sha moves between refreshes — so the read is cold most of the time, exactly when the page is most worth watching.

That is a real problem and it is not this project's (see *Out of scope*). What it forces here is the shape: the refresh cannot be a blocking call in the loop that owns the terminal, and a frame that arrives late must not queue a second one behind it.
**The menu blocks, and that is the thing in the way**

**The menu blocks, and that is the thing in the way.** `menu()` (`src/mc/commands/home.js:121`) is `for (;;) { … await ask(…) }`: it renders, then waits on a line of input, and nothing else can happen in between. A live page needs the reading and the redrawing to be concurrent, with the redraw writing only above the prompt and putting the cursor back where the person left it. That is the whole engineering problem — the differ is arithmetic by comparison.

The page is 87 lines at the current `~/mc`, which is taller than many terminals. So the cursor arithmetic cannot assume the whole page is on screen: only the rows still visible can be addressed, and what has scrolled off is not rewritten and not scrolled back to.

**What the growth case was decided to be, and what it obliges the loop to do.** A frame with more rows than the last one has grown past the footprint it was printed in, and everything below its last row belongs to somebody else — the menu, the blank lines, the prompt — so there is no in-place write that can be right. `frameWrites` answers it with a reprint: up to the page's first row that is still on screen, `CSI 0J` to erase from there to the bottom, then the frame as ordinary lines. The terminal then scrolls at the bottom exactly as the first print of the page scrolled it, which is the only way a line reaches the scrollback once and intact; `CSI L` (insert line) was rejected for the opposite reason — it shifts the region down without scrolling anything into the scrollback and silently drops the bottom row of the screen. The price is on the loop: after a growth frame the cursor is at the end of the last page row, everything below has been erased, and the caller must reprint its own rows and recompute `above`. Every other case comes back to the row it started on.

**The contract, in the two numbers it takes.** `above` is how many rows above the cursor the page's first line sits — with the menu as it stands today that is `lines.length + 4` when the cursor is on the prompt (a blank, the two key lines, a blank). `rows` is the terminal's height and bounds how far up the writes reach: the cursor is assumed to be on the last row of the screen, so `rows - 1` rows above it are addressable and a changed row further up than that is not written at all. That assumption is what keeps a page taller than the terminal safe — a move up past the top row of the screen stops there, so a write meant for a row that has scrolled off would land on a visible one. Left out, `rows` skips nothing, which is right for a test and wrong for a real terminal: the loop should pass it.

**Two things the loop has to carry that the differ cannot.** The column is one: vertical moves keep the column, so the writes return to the row they started on at column 0, and the column a person's half-typed input sits in is only recoverable with a save and a restore around the call. The other is width — `columnsFor` clamps the page to 60 columns minimum, so in a terminal narrower than 60 every page row wraps onto two screen rows and all of this row arithmetic is off by the number of wrapped rows above the cursor. Nothing here detects that; the loop is where it would have to be decided.

A shrinking frame keeps its footprint: the surplus rows are cleared where they stand, so a page that loses rows leaves blank rows above the menu until some later frame grows and reprints. That is deliberate — pulling the rows up with `CSI M` would move the menu and the prompt, which the page does not own — but it is visible, and it is the one place a reader of the finished page might wonder why there is a gap.

steps.title: The loop that does not interrupt the prompt
steps.done_when: `mc` at a terminal refreshes every 30 s while the menu is waiting for input, half-typed input survives, and quitting leaves the terminal as `mc` found it.
instruction: `menu()` in `src/mc/commands/home.js` renders and then blocks on `ask()`. Make the two concurrent: the reader owns the prompt line, the refresh owns everything above it. Before a refresh writes, the cursor is saved; afterwards it is restored to the prompt with whatever the person had typed still there and the cursor at the same column.

The interval is 30 s and it is a floor, not a schedule: the next collect starts 30 s after the previous one *finished*. Never two in flight — the measurement in *What the code taught us* has the collect taking longer than 30 s in the worst case seen, and a queue of frames behind a slow read is how a live page becomes a stale page that also stutters.

A frame that fails — git gone, the work root unreadable, anything `collectPage` can throw — leaves the last good frame on screen and says so in one line rather than tearing the page down. A live surface that blanks on a transient failure is worse than one that says it is holding an old frame.

Terminal resize (`process.stdout.on('resize')`) invalidates the previous frame: the widths were computed for the old columns, so the next write is a full redraw of the page's own rows rather than a diff against lines that no longer describe what is on screen.
Quitting restores the cursor, leaves the last frame in the scrollback, and writes nothing else. `q` and ctrl-c both.

steps.title: A pipe is still a pipe
steps.done_when: Without a TTY, `mc` and `mc --json` print once, exit 0 and emit no escape byte — asserted, not assumed.
instruction: The page already answers this question in two places: `colourFor` refuses colour without a TTY, and `run()` in `commands/home.js` prints and returns rather than calling `menu()`. The live loop hangs off the same fork and must not add a third opinion.

Add the assertion to `tests/mc/front-door.test.js` beside the ones already there: the output of a piped `mc` contains no `\x1b`, and the process exits without waiting. That test is cheap and it is the one that would catch a live surface leaking into a script, a subprocess or a session reading the page.

steps.title: Close it out
steps.done_when: `docs/technical/mc-ui.md` describes the live surface, and `project_log.md` has a row.
instruction: `docs/technical/mc-ui.md` still says `--watch` was removed because a page redrawn on a timer is not a live page, and that the real one is later work. Replace that with what was built: the interval, what is written and what is not, what happens to the scrollback and the prompt, and what a terminal shorter than the page gets.

Say what it costs. The refresh is one `collectPage`, which is the same read a bare `mc` does — and record what it measured while this was built, because the number in that document is from 2026-08-29 and was already an order of magnitude out by 2026-09-02.
